analysis.one_liner: Shields federal disaster-recovery contractors from most private lawsuits over their Gulf Coast work.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced about three weeks after Hurricane Katrina with 8 Republican cosponsors, was placed on the Senate calendar but never received a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: After Hurricane Katrina, this bill would have blocked private lawsuits against contractors doing rescue, cleanup, demolition, and rebuilding work under government contracts, whenever the claim came from federal laws run by the Army, EPA, or Transportation departments. It would have replaced ordinary lawsuits with a new federal process that banned punitive damages, barred pre-judgment interest, required physical injury before pain-and-suffering awards, and reduced payouts by insurance or other compensation already received. It also would have created a strong presumption that contractors who got an Army Corps of Engineers certification were immune from suit, a presumption plaintiffs could overcome only by proving fraud or willful misconduct in the certification process.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction, demolition, debris-removal, and cleanup companies working under federal, state, or local contracts in disaster zones. They would be protected from private lawsuits under a wide set of federal environmental, transportation, and Army-administered laws, and even suits allowed under the bill would face caps on damages and a near-automatic 'government contractor' immunity defense once the Chief of Engineers certified the contract.

how_it_helps.text: Bars private lawsuits against disaster-zone contractors under federal laws administered by the Secretary of the Army, the EPA Administrator, and the Secretary of Transportation [S2] [S3].

Replaces ordinary state-law claims with a single federal cause of action that prohibits punitive damages and pre-judgment interest, limits pain-and-suffering awards to each defendant's share of fault, and requires proof of physical harm before noneconomic damages can be awarded [S3].

Creates a rebuttable presumption of the government contractor defense for contracts the Chief of Engineers certifies as necessary for recovery, and plaintiffs can defeat it only by showing fraud or willful misconduct in the certification process [S3].
Requires payouts to be reduced by any insurance or other collateral-source compensation the plaintiff received for the same loss [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gulf Coast residents whose homes were demolished, property polluted, or families harmed by contractor work would bear the cost: they would lose the right to sue under many federal laws entirely, and the lawsuits still allowed would pay less, on a harder road, in federal court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gulf Coast residents harmed by contractor work

drawbacks.text: The bill would wipe out residents' ability to bring private suits against contractors under federal environmental, transportation, and Army-administered laws, including claims over polluted cleanup sites and flood damage [S2] [S3].

Even for the claims left open, the ban on punitive damages, the collateral-source offset, the physical-injury requirement, and the near-automatic contractor immunity defense would make it much harder and less worthwhile to sue a negligent contractor [S3].
The bill leaves enforcement actions by government agencies intact, meaning contractors would face regulators but not the people they injured, an asymmetry its supporters did not address [S3].
The counterargument supporters offered is that fear of lawsuits raises recovery costs and deters contractors from responding to disasters, a concern stated in the bill's own findings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's premise—that contractors need liability certainty to respond to disasters—had a real basis, but the remedy went far beyond that premise. It would have removed ordinary residents' legal recourse across whole areas of federal law while concentrating the decision about immunity in a single Army official, with a defense so hard to overcome that fraud or willful misconduct in the certification itself would be the only way past it. The savings to taxpayers from lower litigation costs would have come directly out of compensation for people harmed by the recovery work.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2005, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee took it up, no senator ever voted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. John Thune introduced the bill on September 22, 2005, joined by Sens. Vitter, Lott, Murkowski, and Inhofe [S1] [S3].
It was read a second time on September 26, 2005, and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 222 [S1] [S5].
No committee is listed in its history and no further action of any kind followed the placement on the calendar [S5].
The bill never came to a floor vote and died at the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gulf Coast residents came out ahead: they kept their existing right to sue contractors under federal law, and disaster-recovery contractors never received the liability shield or the damages caps the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gulf Coast residents' right to sue

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican, but no vote was ever taken, so the bill's actual level of support or opposition in the full Senate is unknown [S3] [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have exempted them from private lawsuits under federal environmental, transportation, and Army-administered laws and capped the damages available in the suits still allowed, with the savings coming out of compensation for residents they harmed. Their interest in the bill ran directly against the legal rights of the people they would work for.
The bill would have eliminated many private causes of action and sharply limited damages in the remainder, shrinking the cases these lawyers could bring on behalf of Gulf Coast residents.
